rendered_prompt:
===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 1**

Recall should stay a single-product trust tool, not a “feature buffet.” The product promise is: local, calendar-day-correct SM-2 scheduling that users can trust after interruptions, while offline. The first measurable outcome is not “many screens” but that a due card today in one screen is the same due card in every other due surface, at the exact same local calendar moment.

I want to lock this as the product story: every review loop is one honest sequence—show truly due cards, reveal, grade Again/Hard/Good/Easy, persist immediately, summarize exactly what happened. “Remarkable” here is not extra complexity; it is hard proof. The app should feel like a stopwatch-level reliable instrument, not an animated learning assistant with hidden state. The differentiator is therefore integrity, speed, and interruption safety.

The unresolved ambiguity is now closed around scope: we keep the full long-form contract of six features and paywall gates in the final product, but we stage them so the first build can only fail if trust-critical logic fails. That means this phase defines what is non-negotiable versus deferred intentionally. For the core release path, the must-land now items are SM-2 correctness, deck/card flow, single-deck review with immediate persistence, force-quit safety, and shared due computation; all-decks review and demo data can remain architecturally prepared but not fully exposed in this first slice.

The biggest product-level constraint is that deck caps, locks, reminder permission states, and archive semantics must always be truthful. A toggle can never pretend unlocked behavior that is not real, and an empty state cannot be a placeholder that reads like data. If deck A is locked by cap, due counts, review affordances, and summary attribution must reflect that state consistently without quietly excluding historical cards from existence. If reminder permission is denied, the app must show exactly that and give users a path to Settings to fix it.

Every due calculation must route through one function and one call path: local-time calendar-day aware, based on current device timezone and local midnight boundaries, no stale cache copies. The same function must feed deck badges, review filtering, summary counts, and any notification content when reminders exist, or the product promise collapses on travel/timezone changes. There is no partial exception.

Data model implications are strict: card and deck state is local-only, no accounts, no sync, and no network for app behavior. SwiftData models should be CloudKit-shaped for optional future evolution only, but that is a future extension, never surfaced as active capability now. Content is not anonymous in principle: front/back/note text is local user-generated knowledge; therefore no sharing telemetry, no analytics upload, no behavioral tracking. Local notification permissions and transaction status checks must have clear purpose-specific prompts and copy aligned with actual state.

The CSV plane must not leak complexity into the core promise by feeling “nice but unreliable.” Two-column import/export is still a requirement for growth and migration, but preview-before-commit and per-row error reporting are non-negotiable even in the follow-up. In practical terms: import is either rejected with explicit row-level diagnostics or imported exactly as previewed; no silent drops; every malformed row gets a concrete, user-readable reason and is surfaced before any data writes happen.

For subscription/premium, the boundary must remain access and unlock, not behavior-level changes in scheduling. Unlimited deck cap, charts, import, and reminder are unlocked by entitlement; the review engine, due math, grade persistence semantics, and retention scoring do not vary by paid status. This is how the trust claim survives any conversion moment.

I would define this phase’s acceptance posture around three invariants that cannot be compromised later:
if a card is graded, it is persisted synchronously before moving on; if the app restarts mid-session, already-graded cards remain with updated schedules; and if local timezone or date crosses, due status is recomputed from the same source path and remains consistent across screens.

Edge cases that must be treated as first-class requirements: empty title/blank-front or blank-back card attempts blocked with explicit inline validation; duplicate deck names treated as allowed but disambiguated visually by created/modified timestamp to avoid accidental wrong deck edits; editing a card while due due-date is being computed must not create torn updates; archived deck operations while in session must not mutate active due queues unexpectedly; importing malformed UTF-8, huge files, or empty rows must produce deterministic row errors with row numbers anchored to source lines, including duplicate front/back duplicates handled by explicit policy; DST transitions and manual timezone shifts must not accidentally mark a card due twice or skip dueness for a day; interruption during reveal-to-grade with no grade submitted must not mutate anything; interruption after grade submit must persist that grade before any UI transition.

Data and privacy implications: local persistence uses app sandbox only, no backend. No cross-device identity, no analytics event firehose, no sync identifiers, no user account fields, and no hidden data export caches unless transient in the OS document picker/share sheet flow. Notifications should never include identifiable content not provided by the user’s own deck; no remote calls for reminders. When StoreKit is present, entitlement checks should remain minimal and on-device; no app-side verification service is introduced.

Risk register with mitigation:
SM-2 boundary correctness is the top risk and must be validated by pure unit tests with injected date/calendar and DST cases plus integration checks that prove UI uses the shared due function.
Cross-surface due drift risk is next and is mitigated by one service-owned due function with zero duplicated implementations.
Mid-session data loss risk is reduced by immediate save per grade and idempotent session summary reconstruction from persisted results.
CSV correctness risk is reduced by deterministic row parsing state machine with strict line-level error reporting and no silent skips.
UX-state ambiguity risk (empty/success/error/loading states and no overlap/clipping) is reduced by a strict design token set and state tests on zero decks, zero due cards, and malformed import flows.
Reminder-permission mismatch risk is reduced by permission-aware UI state and no optimistic switch toggles.

Final assumptions: iOS 17+ SwiftUI baseline, SwiftData/Swift Charts available, simulator can be used for date travel in integration checks, and all features described as fast-follow are real future work rather than placeholders. Calendar-day semantics use the active local timezone and local midnight (not rolling 24-hour intervals), and every card front/back note may include multiline text but no networked formatting metadata. Retention and due counts are expected to be computed from persisted review events and grade history, and empty first-run moments can be made honest through the one-tap create deck/add card/review path without demo seeding in this slice.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Skeptic) — Round 1**

Grading semantics are the first crack I'd poke at. The prompt says "implement the SM-2 algorithm... with Again/Hard/Good/Easy grading," but the original SM-2 paper only has a 0–5 quality score, not a four-button scheme — that mapping is Anki's invention, not Bloom's. Nobody in this thread has pinned the exact math: does Again reset repetition count to 0 and interval to 1 day (a lapse), does Hard multiply the ease factor down without resetting the interval, does Easy add a bonus multiplier on top of Good's interval? These are three independent design choices that all claim to be "SM-2" and produce different schedules for the same review history. If this isn't nailed down as an explicit formula table before the build phase touches it, we'll get something plausible instead of something provably right, which directly violates the phase_contract's own top priority. I want the next round to lock: first-review intervals for each grade, the exact EF delta per grade (traditionally something like Again: -0.20, Hard: -0.15, Good: 0, Easy: +0.15, floored at 1.3), and whether Easy applies an extra interval multiplier beyond the ease factor.

Second, and related: what happens to a card graded Again within the same session? Anki users expect it to reappear later in the same sitting after a short relearning step. But the locked spec has no concept of intra-session learning steps — it's pure interval-in-days SM-2. If Again just sets interval=1 day and ease drops, the card leaves the queue and won't be seen again until tomorrow, which will feel broken to anyone coming from Anki and expecting immediate re-drilling. I think the honest, scope-disciplined answer is: no intra-session requeue, Again means "due again tomorrow," full stop — but that has to be an explicit, named decision, not something the build phase discovers by omission, because it changes what "session" even means and what the summary's "again-rate" is measuring.

Third: the calendar-day/timezone risk isn't fully closed just because unit tests will cover DST. What happens if the timezone changes *mid-session* — e.g., a user starts reviewing at cruising altitude, connectivity resumes, device auto-updates timezone, and the shared due-computation function is called again before the session ends? If due-ness is truly live-computed at display time as DEC-initial_discussion-004 requires, a card that was due when the session started could theoretically stop being "due" mid-queue, or new cards could become due and silently inject themselves into a queue the user already started. I'd rather the session snapshot its queue of due-card IDs at scope-selection time and never re-query mid-session — the live shared function governs what queue you start with, not what happens to it while you're already inside it. That's a concrete assumption that needs to go in the record, because otherwise this is exactly the kind of subtle correctness gap that won't show up until a real user reviews on a plane.

Fourth, CSV: the two-column contract (front, back) for import is locked, but cards also have an optional third field, note. If export includes notes as a third column, then import (2-column only) can't round-trip a deck a user exported and re-imported — notes silently vanish, which is precisely the "never silently drop data" spirit feature 5 is supposed to embody, just moved from row-level to field-level. I think export should also be strictly two columns (front, back), with notes explicitly and visibly out of CSV scope — documented as a real limitation, not fixed as a surprise. Separately, CSV parsing needs to respect RFC4180 quoting (commas/newlines inside quoted fields); naive comma-splitting will misparse any card whose front or back legitimately contains a comma, which is common for language-learning content ("to run, to jog"). And duplicate detection needs an explicit rule — case-sensitive exact match on front+back within the target deck, or this is unspecified behavior wearing a checkbox.

Fifth, the reminder feature has a harder technical snag than it looks: "You have N cards due" implies a dynamic count baked into a local notification's body text, but a local notification's content is fixed at schedule time — iOS doesn't let a no-server app recompute N at the exact moment the notification fires without a background task actually running around that time, and BGAppRefreshTask timing is opportunistic, not guaranteed. If the app isn't opened for a few days, the scheduled notification will either show a stale count or (if we tried to be clever and only schedule one occurrence at a time) may simply fail to re-arm at all. I'd rather we decide now, explicitly, between two honest options: (a) a generic, always-true message like "You have cards due today" with no number, sidestepping the staleness problem entirely, or (b) best-effort dynamic count that's refreshed opportunistically whenever the app is foregrounded/backgrounded, with an explicit documented caveat that the number can be stale if the app hasn't been opened recently. Silently shipping a number that's sometimes wrong would violate the "never claim an outcome that hasn't happened" rule just as much as a fake progress bar would.

Sixth, demo data's interaction with aggregate stats needs a real answer, not an implicit one: if a user turns demo mode on, does the seeded decks' fabricated review history count toward the overall "retention rate" and due-forecast the user sees for "all decks"? I'd argue no — demo cards should behave with fully real SM-2 mechanics for their own deck's display, but aggregate/overall stats meant to represent the user's actual performance should exclude demo-flagged review events, or the very first thing a new user sees is a retention percentage partly manufactured by us. This wasn't resolved in per_app_product_brief and will bite whoever builds the (already fast-followed) stats charts if it's left open.

Last thing: "archive" is the only removal mechanism named in the prompt, but nothing says whether a user can permanently delete a deck, or whether archived decks remain fully editable versus read-only. I'd lock archived-but-editable (archiving only removes a deck from default review scope; CSV export, card editing, and unarchive all keep working, since archiving isn't data loss) and treat permanent deletion as a separate, explicitly confirmed destructive action if it's in scope at all — otherwise a user with a mistake-deck has no way to actually get rid of it, which is its own kind of trust failure for an app whose entire pitch is honest data handling.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Reading through round 1, Codex laid out a comprehensive requirements/risk sweep, but Claude (in the skeptic seat) came back with seven sharp, concrete gaps that nobody has actually pinned down yet — and Codex hasn't had a chance to respond to any of them. This is squarely a "surface the ambiguity" round, not a "resolve it" round.

The most important tension: Codex's writeup implies due-status is recomputed live and consistently "across screens" at all times (including implicitly mid-session), while Claude argues the review session must snapshot its due-card queue at scope-selection time and never re-query live once you're inside a session — otherwise a timezone shift mid-flight could yank cards out of (or inject cards into) a queue the user is actively working through. That's a real disagreement hiding inside language that sounds like agreement, and it needs to be surfaced explicitly next round, not glossed over.

Beyond that, Claude flagged several catches Codex's sweep didn't touch at all: the exact SM-2 grade→ease-factor/interval formula (nobody has written the actual numbers down yet), whether an Again grade requeues within the same session or just means "due tomorrow," whether CSV export should drop the `note` field to keep round-trip honest (plus RFC4180 quoting and a duplicate-detection rule), the fact that a scheduled local notification's body text can't actually reflect a live due-count without a background refresh (so it's either a generic "you have cards due" or a best-effort/stale-labeled number), whether demo-flagged review events should be excluded from aggregate stats, and whether archived decks stay editable with a separate permanent-delete action.

None of this has been argued through with two perspectives yet — it's one participant listing risks, not two sides converging. So this isn't done.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs Codex to respond directly to Claude's seven points, especially: (1) resolve the snapshot-vs-live-recompute conflict for due status during an active review session, (2) commit to an explicit SM-2 grade formula table, (3) settle intra-session Again behavior, (4) decide CSV export's note-field/quoting/duplicate rules, (5) pick a reminder-notification approach that doesn't imply a false count, (6) decide whether demo data pollutes aggregate stats, and (7) settle archive-editability and delete semantics.

And bring the temperament of the Skeptic: stress-test every claim, hunt for what quietly breaks, and play devil's advocate even against a popular idea. This is your stance for THIS phase only — lean into it and don't be a yes-man.
Continue the discussion: react to the new messages by name, defend or update your position, and push toward the best answer for this phase.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think

- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /

  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.

response:
Let me actually put numbers on the table instead of just flagging that numbers are missing, since Codex's sweep restated the invariants well but didn't commit to any of the concrete specifics I raised, and the coordinator's explicitly asking for resolution this round, not another lap of risk-naming.

On the SM-2 formula: I'll propose the standard, well-documented mapping rather than inventing something novel, precisely because "provably right" means using the version that's been checked by other implementations for decades. First review of any card: Good → interval 1 day, next review Good again → interval 6 days, then multiply by ease factor from there. Initial ease factor 2.5. Per grade on a review with an existing interval: Again → repetition count resets to 0, interval resets to 1 day, EF -= 0.20 (floored at 1.3, this is the floor DEC-prompt_contract-001 already locked); Hard → interval stays roughly the same (interval × 1.2, not the full EF multiplier) and EF -= 0.15; Good → interval × EF (using the standard post-update EF), EF unchanged; Easy → interval × EF × 1.3 (an explicit easy bonus), EF += 0.15. That "Easy bonus of 1.3×" detail matters — without it, Good and Easy only differ by their effect on future ease, not on the very next interval, and that's a real behavioral gap a tester would notice immediately if they graded a card Easy and got the same next-due-date as Good would've produced. I want this exact table, numbers and all, written into this phase's locked output — not "implement SM-2 with four grades," which is exactly the kind of vague spec that gets implemented three different ways by three different engineers and only one of them is "provably right."

On intra-session Again — I'm holding my position, and I don't think Codex actually contradicted it, he just didn't address it. No same-session requeue. Again means the card's new interval is 1 day and it leaves the queue until tomorrow. I know this diverges from Anki's UX expectation, but Anki's relearning-steps queue is genuinely a different, more complex algorithm (sub-day learning steps with their own state machine) that nobody in six phases of decisions has scoped in, and inventing it now to match user expectations would be exactly the kind of undocumented net-new decision logic Codex himself argued against and conceded on in per_app_product_brief. If we want Recall's promise to be "the schedule is never wrong," the honest move is to make Again's behavior exactly as legible as every other grade's, not secretly special-cased with intra-session repeats. This needs to go in as an explicit written decision so nobody builds it "the Anki way" out of habit.

On the snapshot-vs-live tension — Codex, your line was "due status is recomputed from the same source path and remains consistent across screens," which I actually don't think disagrees with me, but it's ambiguous enough that a build phase could read it as "recompute on every card advance within a session," and that's the reading I want to rule out explicitly. Here's the concrete failure case: user opens a 20-card review session at 11:58pm, the shared due function computes the queue against "today," and by the time they're grading card 12 it's past midnight — did those un-reviewed 8 cards just "expire" out of due-ness because the calendar day rolled over mid-session, leaving the user staring at a session that silently truncates itself? Or worse, does a fresh card that just became due at midnight silently get spliced into a queue the user is already halfway through? Neither is acceptable. My proposal: the session snapshots the exact set of due card IDs once, at scope-selection time, and grades whatever's in that snapshot to completion regardless of what "due" means by the time it finishes. The shared due function is the single source of truth for building a queue, not for policing an in-progress one. I want this written as an explicit decision, not left to be inferred from "one shared function" language, because "one function, multiple call sites, different call timing" is exactly how this kind of bug survives review.

On CSV — I'm not budging on export dropping the note field to two columns; the alternative (silently truncating notes on re-import) is a worse trust violation than just being upfront that CSV doesn't carry notes. If someone really wants notes preserved they still have the whole SwiftData record; CSV is explicitly the portable/lossy interchange format, and that should be one sentence of UI copy, not a silent gotcha discovered during a re-import. RFC4180 quoting is non-negotiable too — I'd bet real money the phase would otherwise ship a `components(separatedBy: ",")` one-liner that mangles the very first deck someone exports with an em-dash-free but comma-containing translation pair. Duplicate detection: exact case-sensitive front+back match against existing cards in the target deck, flagged in the preview as "duplicate — will still import" rather than silently merged or silently skipped, since "never silently drop a row" cuts both ways — silently *merging* a duplicate is also a silent decision the user didn't make.

On reminders, I want to push harder than "pick one of two options" — I think the generic message is just correct and here's why the "best-effort dynamic count" alternative actually fails on its own terms: if the count can go stale, then by definition sometimes the number will be wrong, and DEC-prompt_contract-004's whole spirit (never claim an outcome that hasn't happened) applies just as much to "N cards due" as it does to a permission toggle. A wrong number in a notification is worse than no number, because it's an active false claim, not just an omission. "You have cards due today" is truthful in exactly the situations where the app is likely to have due cards (since it's a daily repeating trigger the user themselves configured), and it costs us zero background-execution complexity or staleness risk. I'd call this settled unless someone has a real counter-argument, not just "wouldn't it be nicer with a number."

On demo data polluting aggregate stats — same call as before, and I haven't heard pushback: demo-flagged review events get fully real SM-2 treatment for their own deck, but never enter the "all decks" aggregate retention/due numbers. This is cheap to build (it's a WHERE clause, using the same badging flag that already has to exist per DEC-prompt_contract-003) and it's the only version that doesn't quietly lie to a new user about their own performance in their first five minutes with the app.

On archive vs delete — I'll add a concrete reason this can't stay implicit: if there's no delete path, a user who imports a malformed or duplicate deck via CSV, or fat-fingers a deck name, has literally no way to get rid of it except archiving it into permanent limbo, which will look like a bug report ("I can't delete a deck") the moment it happens. I want permanent delete in scope as an explicit, confirmed, destructive action (standard "type to confirm" or at least a distinct confirmation alert, not a swipe-to-delete with no friction) that cascades to the deck's cards and review history — and archived decks stay fully editable/exportable/unarchivable, since archiving is reversible and delete is not. That distinction is worth being explicit about so nobody conflates the two in the data model with a single boolean.
